name: Hebrew (Modern Israeli)
variety: General (non-Oriental) Modern Israeli Hebrew: no pharyngeals, uvular rhotic. The Oriental variety, with /ħ ʕ/ and an alveolar trill, is noted where it differs.
sources: Laufer, Asher (1990). Hebrew. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 20(2): 40-43. Reprinted in the Handbook of the International Phonetic Association, Cambridge University Press, 1999.
Bolozky, Shmuel (1997). Israeli Hebrew phonology. In Alan S. Kaye (ed.), Phonologies of Asia and Africa, vol. 1. Winona Lake: Eisenbrauns.
Most, Tova, Amir, Ofer & Tobin, Yishai (2000). The Hebrew vowel system: raw and normalized acoustic data. Language and Speech 43(3): 295-308.
Silber-Varod, Vered, Sagi, Hagit & Amir, Noam (2016). The acoustic correlates of lexical stress in Israeli Hebrew. Journal of Phonetics 56: 1-14.
Cohen, Evan-Gary, Silber-Varod, Vered & Amir, Noam (2018). The acoustics of primary and secondary stress in Modern Hebrew. Brill's Journal of Afroasiatic Languages and Linguistics 10: 1-19.
Bat-El, Outi, Cohen, Evan-Gary & Silber-Varod, Vered (2019). Modern Hebrew stress: phonology and phonetics. Brill's Journal of Afroasiatic Languages and Linguistics 11(1): 96-118.
Asherov, Daniel & Cohen, Evan-Gary (2019). A phonetic description of Modern Hebrew consonants and vowels. Brill's Journal of Afroasiatic Languages and Linguistics 11(1).
Silber-Varod, Vered & Amir, Noam (2021). Prosodic properties of Hebrew word-level stress: high-low or long-short? Conference abstract, Tone and Intonation 2021.

Raphael, Lawrence J., Tobin, Yishai, Faber, Alice, Most, Tova, Kollia, H. Betty & Milstein, Doron (1995). Intermediate values of voice onset time. In Fredericka Bell-Berti & Lawrence J. Raphael (eds.), Producing Speech: Contemporary Issues. New York: AIP Press.
Berkovits, Rochele (1994). Durational effects in final lengthening, gapping, and contrastive stress. Language and Speech 37: 237-250.
Graf, Dafna & Ussishkin, Adam (2003). Emergent iambs: stress in Modern Hebrew. Lingua 113: 239-270.
Dekel, Nurit (2014). Colloquial Israeli Hebrew: A Corpus-based Survey. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton.
contrasts: place of stress: ˈboker 'morning' against boˈker 'cowboy', ˈberex 'knee' against beˈrex 'he blessed'
stops against fricatives /p f/, /b v/, /k χ/; the pairs alternate within verb and noun paradigms but are separate phonemes
five vowel qualities, no vowel length, no gemination in the general variety
/tʃ dʒ ʒ w/ occur in loanwords and names only
allophony: /p t k/ are slightly aspirated; /b d ɡ/ are voiced throughout the closure. Reported voice onset times are a short to intermediate lag of roughly 20 to 45 ms for the voiceless stops, longest for /k/, and a lead of roughly 75 to 100 ms for the voiced stops (Raphael et al. 1995 and later work; approximate)
/ʁ/ is a uvular approximant [ʁ̞], for some speakers a uvular trill; Oriental speakers have an alveolar trill or tap
/χ/ is a voiceless uvular fricative, usually with uvular trilling
/ʔ/ and /h/ are often dropped, most of all in unstressed syllables and fast speech; /h/ between vowels is voiced [ɦ]
two like vowels brought together by the loss of /ʔ/ or /h/ are spoken as one long vowel in casual speech
vowels and consonants are longer in stressed syllables and longer still at the end of a sense group; unstressed vowels are shorter and centralised (Laufer 1990)
/e/ is diphthongised to [ej] in some words; the diphthongs are vowel plus /j/ sequences
the mid vowels are true mid [e̞ o̞] and /a/ is central
regressive voicing assimilation in obstruent clusters
Oriental variety only: /ħ/ for historical ḥet and /ʕ/ for ʿayin, gemination in careful speech, more pronounced mobile shva
phonotactics: word-initial clusters of two consonants are common
an initial cluster whose first member is a sonorant, or whose members are alike, is broken by an epenthetic /e/ (the pronounced shva)
final clusters occur in loanwords and in second person feminine past forms in -t
before a word-final historical guttural a low vowel is inserted after a non-low vowel: /ˈʁuaχ/ 'wind' (furtive pataḥ)
no geminates; a shva between two identical consonants is pronounced /e/ (ʃodeˈdim 'robbers')

stress.rule: Stress is final by default and penultimate in segolate nouns (ˈmelex, ˈsefer), before the unstressed past tense suffixes -ti, -ta, -t, -nu (kaˈtavti), and in many loanwords, names and colloquial forms; antepenultimate stress is found in loanwords only.
stress.cues: vowel duration is the main cue, intensity a weaker one, and F0 plays a minor part (Silber-Varod, Sagi & Amir 2016); secondary stress has no consistent acoustic realisation (Cohen, Silber-Varod & Amir 2018)

rhythm.vowel_reduction: moderate: unstressed vowels are shorter and centralised and unstressed /e/ may be dropped in fast speech; no phonological reduction to schwa
rhythm.notes: No rhythm-metric classification is cited here. Syllables are fairly even and every vowel keeps its quality, but stress lengthens and clusters are frequent. Utterance-final vowels lengthen whether stressed or not, the stressed ones more (Silber-Varod & Amir 2021; Berkovits 1994).

length.notes: No contrastive length. Stressed vowels are longer than unstressed ones and phrase-final syllables are longer still. Long vowels arise only from the fusion of two like vowels; geminates only in careful Oriental speech.

intonation.declarative: pitch accents on the stressed syllables of content words; in non-final words pitch rises through the word so that its last syllable is the highest; the last content word carries the nuclear accent, followed by a fall to a low boundary
intonation.yes_no_question: word order of a statement (optionally with the particle haʔim); the final word ends in a rise to a high boundary
intonation.wh_question: peak on the question word, then a fall to a low end
intonation.continuation: rise or sustained high pitch at the end of each non-final phrase
intonation.accent_shape: rising accent with a late peak before the nucleus; falling nuclear accent
intonation.notes: In phrase-medial words of two syllables F0 is higher on the second vowel whatever the stress pattern, and utterance-final vowels have lowered F0: F0 marks the phrase and duration marks the word stress (Silber-Varod & Amir 2021). The sentence-type descriptions are general statements, not an autosegmental analysis.

problems: The rules read pointed text. Ordinary unpointed words that are not in he_list or he_listx (about 300 entries) are spoken as consonant strings with no vowels, apart from a few endings: מלך gives [mlχ], דבר [dvr], בוקר [vvkr], כתבתי [χtvtˈi].

Pointed words are recognised only when the marks come in the order listed in he_rules. With the Unicode canonical order (vowel point before dagesh or shin dot), or with a combination that is not listed (bet + dagesh + holam), the word is spelled out letter by letter with 'Invalid phoneme code' errors: שָׁלוֹם, דָּבָר, יַלְדָּה, בֹּקֶר.
No stress rule is set, so the default penultimate stress applies, but Hebrew stress is mostly final: דָּבָר gives ˈdavar, גָּדוֹל ˈɡadol, חָבֵר ˈχaver, שָׁלוֹם ˈʃalom.
Final vowel letters are pronounced as consonants in pointed words: יַלְדָּה ends in [h] and אֲנִי ends in [j].
Furtive pataḥ is read after the consonant: רוּחַ gives [ˈruχa] for [ˈʁuaχ].
/r/ is the alveolar trill R of the base table, not the uvular [ʁ] of the general variety.
The he phoneme table is empty: all vowels and consonants are the generic base ones, without the lengthening of stressed and phrase-final vowels described by Laufer.
No elision of /h/ and /ʔ/, no voicing assimilation, no language-specific intonation.
good: χ, ts, tʃ, dʒ and ʒ are available, and the letters with geresh (ג׳ ז׳ צ׳) are read
ʿayin is merged with the glottal stop and ḥet with χ, as in the general variety
segolate nouns with pointing get the right penultimate stress (סֵפֶר, מֶלֶךְ)
numbers and letter names are defined in he_list

notes: Vowel formants for men, women and children are published in Most, Amir & Tobin (2000); no values are given here because they could not be checked against the source. The voice onset time ranges in the allophony list are approximate and therefore not given as a numeric block.
